title: 33 Dose-dependent impacts of thymol on rumen microbial populations in beef steers fed forage analyzed via whole genome shotgun sequencing
content:
Abstract
While essential oils (EO) are gaining momentum as a strategy to reduce enteric methane emissions in cattle, little is known about how their bioactive components, terpenes, affect rumen microbial populations when consumed at various doses. Thymol is a low molecular weight terpenoid present in thyme and oregano EO with broad and potent antimicrobial activity. Due to the efficacy of thymol, in vitro research has established that thymol >500 mg/L rumen fluid impairs fermentation activities, possibly through disrupting microbial cell membranes. The objective of this research was to determine the effects of increasing doses of thymol on rumen microbial populations in beef steers using whole genome shotgun sequencing (WGS) with the overarching aim of utilizing viable doses that would not negatively impact forage utilization. We utilized four beef steers in a 4×4 Latin square with four 14-d periods. Four doses of thymol (0 [CON], 120 [120-T], 240 [240-T], and 480 [480-T] mg thymol/kg intake) were administered on alfalfa cubes with a basal forage diet provided ad libitum. Rumen contents were collected then separated into liquid and solid fractions on d 14 of each period. Between each experimental period, there were 14-d washout periods to allow rumen microbial populations to return to baseline. DNA was extracted from liquid and solid rumen contents and analyzed via WGS and statistical analyses tested for orthogonal contrasts. For the liquid rumen environment, there was a quadratic effect of thymol on Prevotella sp. (P=0.01) and a linear effect on uncultured Prevotella sp. (P=0.05), with the lowest abundance for animals receiving 120-T, and the highest for animals receiving 240-T. Several low abundance liquid-associated microbial species (< 1% relative abundance) were linearly and quadratically impacted by thymol doses (P£0.05), distributed in the following phyla: 11 in Bacillota, five in Pseudomonadota, three in actinobacteria, and three in Bacteroidota. For the solid rumen environment, thymol had a quadratic effect on Butyrivibrio sp. and uncultured Clostridiales bacterium, where CON steers had the highest relative abundance of each (P£0.05). Thymol also quadratically affected uncultured Lachnospiraceae bacterium, and uncultured Methanobrevibacter sp. in the solid environment (P£0.05), where 240-T steers had the highest relative abundance for uncultured Lachnospiraceae bacterium, and 120-T for uncultured Methanobrevibacter sp. In the solid rumen environment, two archaeal and 28 bacterial low abundance species were linearly and quadratically impacted by thymol (P£0.05); 17 in the phylum Bacillota, six in the phylum Pseudomonadota, two in the phylum Spirochaete, two in Euryarchaeota, and one in each of the following phyla: Bacteriodota, Chloroflexi, and Elusimicrobiota. These data indicate that the antimicrobial effects of terpenes are dose-dependent and most commonly display a quadratic, rather than a linear effect on microbial species, at the doses provided in this study, particularly for species involved in carbohydrate metabolism.
